data.question: Should we adopt the rule change block_k 3 → 2, which raises on-time deliveries but which Companies B and C voted against, or keep the current rules (v2)?
data.background: Option 1 passed cadl check and the constitution, and it improves the main goal on_time_deliveries by +1.6. It failed the company vote: A voted for it, B and C voted against. Adopting it would mean overriding two of the three companies, and only 2 of 5 seeds improved, so the gain is not clearly robust. Weighing customer gains against the companies' losses and their vote is a judgment for a human, not for me.

options.summary: Robots waiting behind a parked robot trigger its eviction once two are waiting instead of three. On-time rises from 223.6 to 225.2 (+1.6), but only 2/5 seeds improved. Late falls from 4.4 to 2.8, and blocked s falls from 915 to 682. The lowest on-time rate rises from 0.96 to 0.98. Customer monitors all improve or hold: p95_wait_s 116 → 108, max_wait_s 154 → 141, unfinished stays at 0.0. Road violations rise from 18.2 to 24.0. Utility moves from 73.8 / 69.8 / 58.2 to 73.8 / 61.4 / 46.0. Votes were A ○, B ×, C ×, so adopting it means overriding B and C.
options.stakeholders: Customers gain: fewer late deliveries and shorter typical and worst-case waits, with no loss on any customer monitor. Company A is unaffected (utility 73.8). Company B loses (69.8 → 61.4). Company C loses the most (58.2 → 46.0), on top of its earlier loss from D1 (28.8 → 19.2 in period 1). Other road users face more road violations (18.2 → 24.0). Overriding a majority 'no' vote may also weaken the companies' trust in the rule process.

options.summary: Stay at v2. Current values remain: on-time 223.6, late 4.4, blocked s 915, road violations 18.2, lowest on-time rate 0.96. Customer monitors stay at p95_wait_s 116, max_wait_s 154 and unfinished 0.0. Utility stays at 73.8 / 69.8 / 58.2.
options.stakeholders: Companies B and C keep their current utility, and their vote is respected. Customers forgo the measured improvements: about 1.6 fewer on-time deliveries, 1.6 more late deliveries, and longer waits (p95 116 vs 108, max 154 vs 141). Road violations stay lower. Company A is indifferent.

recommendation.reason: Option 1's mean gain on the main goal (+1.6) is small, and it improved on only 2 of 5 seeds, so a majority of seeds did not improve. That is weak evidence for overriding a majority 'no' vote by B and C, whose utility falls sharply (C 58.2 → 46.0, after an earlier loss in D1). It would also raise road violations by about 30%. The customer gains are real but modest, and the current rules already deliver 223.6 on time with 0.0 unfinished. I recommend keeping v2 and re-measuring option 1 with more seeds. A human may reasonably choose option 1 instead if the customer wait improvements are judged decisive under the KPI.
assumptions: The 2/5 seed result reflects real variance rather than a consistent small gain hidden by noise.
The increase in road violations does not itself harm customers beyond what the measured wait metrics show.
B's and C's votes reflect their utility losses and not strategic voting.
Fairness between companies is still outside the KPI as written (K1), but repeated losses for C are worth weighing.

unknowns: Whether the +1.6 on-time gain holds over more seeds, or whether it is driven by a few seeds.
How customers weigh shorter waits (p95 −8 s, max −13 s) against the change, and whether they notice it at all.
Why B and C lose utility: more evictions of their parked robots, or longer routes.
How B and C would change their behaviour, such as parking strategy, if option 1 were imposed against their vote.
Next period's demand level, and whether congestion, and so the value of earlier eviction, will grow or shrink.
Whether the higher road violations affect safety or other road users in ways not captured in the table.
Whether another block_k value or a combined change could keep the customer gains with smaller losses for B and C.
